title: Pleural Disorders, Pneumothorax & Chest Tubes: Recognition, Drainage and Emergency Response
html:
Pleural disease can impair ventilation even when the airways and alveoli are initially intact. Air, blood, fluid, pus, or lymph in the pleural space separates the lung from the chest wall and can restrict expansion. The RN must recognize respiratory compromise, identify tension physiology without waiting for late signs, maintain a safe closed-drainage system, and respond to sudden client or device changes without creating a new hazard.

Learning goals

  • Explain how negative pleural pressure supports lung expansion.
  • Differentiate simple, open, and tension pneumothorax and recognize obstructive shock.
  • Compare pneumothorax, hemothorax, pleural effusion, empyema, and chylothorax.
  • Assess chest-drain function using the client, insertion site, tubing, and device together.
  • Interpret tidaling, bubbling, suction indicators, and drainage trends in context.
  • Respond safely to deterioration, disconnection, accidental removal, and suspected obstruction.
  • Teach mobility, respiratory recovery, recurrence prevention, and urgent warning signs.

The pleural space couples lung to chest wall

The visceral pleura covers the lung and the parietal pleura lines the chest wall. A thin lubricated space lies between them. Normally negative intrapleural pressure helps keep the lung expanded as the chest wall moves. When air or fluid enters, that pressure relationship is disrupted and the lung may partially or completely collapse.

Severity is not predicted by radiographic size alone. A small pneumothorax can be dangerous in a client with limited cardiopulmonary reserve, and positive-pressure ventilation can accelerate air accumulation. Assess respiratory effort, oxygenation, hemodynamics, comorbid disease, mechanism, and trend.

Recognize pneumothorax from the clinical pattern

Pneumothorax may be primary spontaneous, secondary to underlying lung disease, traumatic, or iatrogenic after a procedure such as central venous access, lung biopsy, thoracentesis, or positive-pressure ventilation. Common findings include sudden pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachypnea, tachycardia, reduced chest movement, and decreased or absent breath sounds on the affected side. Hyperresonance can occur but may be difficult to appreciate.

Stable suspected pneumothorax is usually confirmed with chest imaging or bedside ultrasound and managed according to symptoms, physiology, cause, size, resources, and recurrence risk. Do not assume every client requires the same intervention; observation, aspiration, ambulatory devices, or tube drainage may be selected by the treating team.

Tension pneumothorax is a bedside emergency

In tension pneumothorax, air enters but cannot escape. Rising intrapleural pressure collapses the affected lung, shifts intrathoracic structures, reduces venous return, and can cause obstructive shock and cardiac arrest. Sudden respiratory distress, unilateral markedly reduced breath sounds, tachycardia, hypotension, worsening hypoxemia, distended neck veins, or rapid deterioration—especially during positive-pressure ventilation—should trigger immediate concern.

Do not wait for tracheal deviation or an x-ray
Tracheal shift can be late or absent. When tension physiology is suspected in an unstable client, activate emergency response, support oxygenation and ventilation, and prepare for immediate decompression by an authorized clinician. Imaging must not delay lifesaving treatment.

Open pneumothorax and traumatic chest injury

An open chest wound allows air to move between the environment and pleural space. Cover the wound using the emergency dressing approach specified by the trauma protocol, provide oxygen and rapid escalation, and monitor for worsening tension physiology. Do not probe the wound or remove an embedded object.

Trauma can also cause hemothorax, pulmonary contusion, rib injury, flail chest, or cardiac tamponade. Hemothorax may produce decreased breath sounds, dullness rather than hyperresonance, tachycardia, hypotension, and shock. Treat airway, breathing, and circulation together; a chest finding does not exclude major blood loss.

Pleural fluid requires a cause, not just a drain

Pleural effusion is excess fluid in the pleural space. Causes include heart failure, infection, malignancy, liver or kidney disease, and pulmonary embolism. Findings can include dyspnea, pleuritic discomfort, reduced breath sounds, decreased fremitus, and dullness to percussion. Imaging identifies location and volume; sampled fluid helps distinguish mechanisms and guide treatment.

Empyema is infected purulent pleural fluid and often requires antimicrobial therapy plus drainage. Chylothorax contains lymphatic fluid and may cause nutritional and immune losses. Hemothorax contains blood and can threaten both ventilation and circulation. Trend the client's status and the drainage character, not appearance alone.

Thoracentesis needs preparation and reassessment

Before thoracentesis, verify the order, identity, consent process, relevant imaging and laboratory data, anticoagulant or bleeding risk, allergies, baseline respiratory assessment, and monitoring plan. Position as directed—often upright leaning forward when tolerated—while maintaining safety and stillness. Use sterile technique and label specimens accurately.

Afterward, reassess breath sounds, respiratory effort, oxygenation, pain, vital signs, puncture site, and any ordered imaging. Sudden dyspnea, chest pain, hypoxemia, tachycardia, hypotension, or unilateral breath-sound loss may indicate pneumothorax, bleeding, or another complication and requires prompt escalation. Rapid removal of a large volume can rarely contribute to re-expansion pulmonary edema, so follow prescribed limits and monitor the clinical response.

Understand the chest-drain system

A chest tube removes air or fluid and allows pleural pressure to recover. The collection chamber receives drainage; the water-seal or one-way mechanism prevents air from returning to the chest; and the suction-control component regulates applied suction when prescribed. Device design varies, so identify the exact system and follow its manufacturer instructions and facility policy.

Keep the drainage unit upright and below the insertion site. Secure connections, preserve the occlusive dressing, and arrange tubing without compression, kinks, or dependent loops that obstruct flow. Confirm that suction is set as prescribed. Increasing wall suction beyond the device's regulated setting does not necessarily increase suction at the pleural space and may create noise or harm.

Assess the client before interpreting the chambers

Trend breathing, oxygenation, lung sounds, chest movement, pain, hemodynamics, subcutaneous emphysema, insertion-site condition, drainage amount and character, tubing path, water-seal behavior, suction indicator, and prescribed settings. Mark drainage level with date and time when required and report a sudden unexpected increase, bright-red output, abrupt cessation with symptoms, or output beyond protocol thresholds.

Do not strip or milk tubing routinely because large negative pressures can be generated. Do not clamp a bubbling chest tube or routinely clamp for transport unless a specific authorized order, device instruction, or emergency protocol requires it. Clamping can trap air and precipitate tension pneumothorax.

Tidaling and bubbling require context

Water-seal tidaling—movement with respiration—often indicates pressure transmission through a patent system. Its absence can mean the lung has re-expanded, but it can also reflect a kink, obstruction, dependent loop, closed clamp, disconnection, or position. Assess the client and trace the system rather than declaring either success or failure from tidaling alone.

Intermittent bubbling in the water seal may occur as pleural air exits early in treatment. Continuous bubbling commonly suggests an air leak from the client, insertion site, connection, or device. Inspect the dressing and connections and follow the approved troubleshooting pathway; do not repeatedly clamp the tube to hunt for a leak unless authorized. Bubbling in a wet-suction control chamber may be expected, while dry-suction devices use a different indicator—know which chamber and device you are viewing.

Device findings never outrank deterioration
A client with new distress, hypotension, hypoxemia, asymmetric breath sounds, or rapidly expanding subcutaneous emphysema needs immediate ABC assessment and escalation even if the drainage unit appears normal.

Respond to sudden drainage-system problems

If the tubing disconnects, stay with and assess the client, apply oxygen as indicated, call for assistance, preserve sterility, and promptly reconnect to a new sterile drainage system according to the device and facility emergency protocol. Temporary measures differ by system and organization; do not improvise prolonged clamping or place the tube into an unapproved container.

If the chest tube is pulled out of the client, cover the site immediately with a sterile occlusive dressing as directed by the emergency protocol, call for urgent help, support breathing, and monitor for recurrent or tension pneumothorax. Do not attempt to reinsert the tube. If the tube is partially displaced, stabilize it, do not advance it, and notify the responsible clinician immediately.

If the unit tips over, return it upright, assess whether water-seal integrity and chamber levels remain correct, and replace the system if required. If the tubing or device is damaged, use the approved emergency pathway and a new sterile system. Document the event, assessments, actions, response, and notifications.

Prevent accidental traction and infection

Use a secure dressing and tube-anchoring method, keep tubing supported during repositioning, and place the system where it cannot be kicked, lifted above the chest, or caught in bed rails. Plan mobility with adequate staff and portable suction when prescribed. Never use the drainage tubing as a handle.

Perform hand hygiene and use aseptic technique for dressing and system care. Inspect for redness, warmth, swelling, drainage, odor, fever, increasing pain, or loss of dressing integrity. Minimize unnecessary system opening because the closed pathway protects the pleural space.

Removal requires coordination

Before removal, verify the order and readiness criteria, explain the breathing instruction selected by the operator, provide analgesia as appropriate, prepare an occlusive dressing, and position safely. During removal, help the client perform the instructed breath hold, Valsalva maneuver, or exhalation without substituting a different technique.

After removal, inspect the sealed dressing and assess respiratory effort, oxygenation, breath sounds, pain, vital signs, and signs of recurrent pneumothorax. Report drainage through the dressing, sudden dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, or asymmetric findings promptly.

Prepare discharge and recurrence teaching

Teach wound care, medication use, activity progression, pulmonary hygiene, follow-up imaging, and when to seek emergency care. Sudden chest pain, new or worsening breathlessness, cyanosis, syncope, rapid heart rate, or falling oxygen saturation requires urgent evaluation.

Smoking increases recurrence risk and cessation support is important. Air travel, high altitude, scuba diving, heavy exertion, and return to work require condition-specific clearance after radiographic resolution and specialist review; do not give a universal waiting period. Clients with recurrent or secondary pneumothorax may need pleurodesis or surgical evaluation.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Assess onset, mechanism, work of breathing, oxygenation, bilateral breath sounds, chest movement, percussion, hemodynamics, neck veins, pain, subcutaneous air, imaging, and device findings.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish air from fluid, stable pneumothorax from tension physiology, expected drainage behavior from leak or obstruction, and respiratory compromise from combined hemorrhagic shock.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, airway compromise, severe hypoxemia, shock, accidental tube removal, and acute obstruction outrank routine chamber troubleshooting.
  4. Generate solutions: Support ABCs, activate emergency help, prepare decompression or drainage, protect the insertion pathway, restore a sterile closed system, and obtain prescribed imaging and monitoring.
  5. Take action: Treat the client before the device, avoid unsafe clamping or manipulation, maintain the unit below the chest, and follow device-specific and organizational emergency procedures.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess breathing, oxygen need, bilateral sounds, hemodynamics, pain, drainage trend, air leak, tidaling, insertion site, imaging, mobility, and teach-back.

Clinical example

A mechanically ventilated client suddenly becomes hypotensive and hypoxemic, with rapidly rising airway pressure and absent breath sounds on the right. The RN recognizes possible tension pneumothorax, activates emergency response, provides oxygen and ventilation support, checks for immediately reversible equipment problems without delaying care, and prepares for bedside decompression and chest-tube placement. After intervention, the RN reassesses bilateral breath sounds, oxygenation, blood pressure, airway pressure, tube position, water-seal behavior, drainage, and subcutaneous emphysema.
